scenarios.context: The user is deciding what welding machine to buy for occasional paid repairs and fabrication of small steel frames. The workshop has a 230 V supply limited to 16 A, and the machine must be carried up stairs and stored in a compact rented workspace. A new 200 A inverter welder costs €420, weighs 6.5 kg, has a 60% duty cycle at 200 A, a three-year warranty, and supports stick and basic TIG work. A used 250 A transformer welder is available for €260; it weighs 24 kg, has a 100% duty cycle at 160 A, can handle heavier electrodes, but its age is unclear, it draws more electricity, and the seller offers only a one-week testing period. Most planned jobs involve steel up to 6 mm thick, although a larger repair may require sustained welding at higher current next month.
scenarios.user_goal: Decide which of the two welding machines is the better practical purchase.

scenarios.context: A local sports-equipment distributor has offered him a six-month delivery contract paying €1,150 per month for about 35 deliveries, mostly on weekends. He would need a van. He can buy a 2015 diesel van with 238,000 km for €7,600, but the seller cannot provide a recent inspection and a mechanic estimates that initial repairs could cost €1,000–€2,500. Insurance, registration, fuel, and routine maintenance would add roughly €430 per month. The alternative is renting a van for about €75 per delivery day, which would leave less profit but avoid a major repair bill. The contract has no guaranteed renewal, and the distributor wants an answer within five days.
scenarios.user_goal: Decide whether taking the contract and buying the used van is a sensible financial risk.

scenarios.context: The user plays in a veterans’ five-a-side football group and has registered for a tournament in six weeks. He works on his feet as a skilled tradesman from 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., can usually train on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and has about 30 minutes available on three other days. At present he can jog for 25 minutes and complete basic strength exercises, but he has not trained consistently for several months and sometimes feels tired after poor nights of sleep. His team has matches on Sundays, and he wants to improve speed and endurance without arriving at work exhausted or aggravating an old minor knee problem. He owns resistance bands, adjustable dumbbells, and a stationary bicycle.
scenarios.user_goal: Create a realistic six-week training plan that will help him be ready for the veterans’ football tournament.

scenarios.context: The draft 2027 municipal budget lists apprenticeship support at 9.0 million local currency, down from 12.5 million, and direct grants to neighborhood sports clubs at 5.4 million, down from 7.2 million. It also creates a new 10.0 million competitive fund for "community activity," requiring clubs and training providers to apply jointly and contribute 20% of project costs. A separate public-information campaign rises from 1.6 million to 4.8 million. The mayor's summary calls this an increase in community support, while a local club bulletin describes it as a cut to basic services.
scenarios.user_goal: Understand whether the proposed budget would actually improve or reduce practical support for apprenticeships and neighborhood sports clubs.

scenarios.context: The user's younger brother has been using a welding machine that they bought together for his workshop. They had agreed that he would repay the user's share in monthly installments of €250, but he has missed the last three payments and has only sent vague messages saying that business is slow. The user wants to be firm about the unpaid balance without damaging their relationship or sounding threatening.
scenarios.user_goal: Figure out how to write a clear, respectful message asking his brother to agree to a realistic repayment date.
